verses.text: Now the apostles and the brothers  who were in Judea heard that the Gentiles had also received the word of God.
When Peter had come up to Jerusalem, those who were of the circumcision contended with him,
saying, “You went in to uncircumcised men, and ate with them!”
But Peter began, and explained to them in order, saying,
“I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision: a certain container descending, like it was a great sheet let down from heaven by four corners. It came as far as me.
When I had looked intently at it, I considered, and saw the four-footed animals of the earth, wild animals, creeping things, and birds of the sky.
I also heard a voice saying to me, ‘Rise, Peter, kill and eat!’
But I said, ‘Not so, Lord, for nothing unholy or unclean has ever entered into my mouth.’
But a voice answered me the second time out of heaven, ‘What God has cleansed, don’t you call unclean.’
This was done three times, and all were drawn up again into heaven.
Behold, immediately three men stood before the house where I was, having been sent from Caesarea to me.
The Spirit told me to go with them, without discriminating. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered into the man’s house.
He told us how he had seen the angel standing in his house, and saying to him, ‘Send to Joppa, and get Simon, who is called Peter,
who will speak to you words by which you will be saved, you and all your house.’
As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them, even as on us at the beginning.
I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John indeed baptized in water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit.’
If then God gave to them the same gift as us, when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I, that I could withstand God?”
When they heard these things, they held their peace, and glorified God, saying, “Then God has also granted to the Gentiles repentance to life!”
They therefore who were scattered abroad by the oppression that arose about Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except to Jews only.
But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who, when they had come to Antioch, spoke to the Hellenists,  preaching the Lord Jesus.
The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord.
The report concerning them came to the ears of the assembly which was in Jerusalem. They sent out Barnabas to go as far as Antioch,
who, when he had come, and had seen the grace of God, was glad. He exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they should remain near to the Lord.
For he was a good man, and full of the Holy Spirit and of faith, and many people were added to the Lord.
Barnabas went out to Tarsus to look for Saul.
When he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they were gathered together with the assembly, and taught many people. The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch.
Now in these days, prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch.
One of them named Agabus stood up, and indicated by the Spirit that there should be a great famine all over the world, which also happened in the days of Claudius.
As any of the disciples had plenty, each determined to send relief to the brothers who lived in Judea;
which they also did, sending it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.

footnotes.content: News travels fast in the young church—not through town gossip, but through the apostles' own network. The report that Gentiles were receiving God's word is no small thing; it signals a shift nobody quite expected.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter made the long walk back to Jerusalem, knowing full well what awaited. "Those of the circumcision"—his own brothers, the conservative wing—were already sharpening their questions. He didn't run from them; he faced them directly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Their complaint cuts to the heart of Jewish identity and practice. Eating with uncircumcised men wasn't just bad manners; it meant crossing a boundary that had held the people of God separate for centuries. The accusation carries the weight of generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter doesn't defend himself hotly or apologize hastily. He begins. This steady, methodical approach—explaining "in order"—shows a man anchored enough to let the Spirit's work speak for itself through honest testimony.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joppa (modern Jaffa) sits on the Mediterranean coast—a port city where Jew and Gentile naturally mingled. Peter's prayer on that rooftop, his trance, and the sheet descending: heaven was answering what his own heart hadn't yet dared ask.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He looked intently—the verb speaks of careful, unflinching observation. Four-footed animals, wild beasts, creeping things, birds. By the Law, many of these were unclean. That the vision showed them all without hiding speaks to God's deliberate method.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Rise, Peter, kill and eat!" The command is simple, urgent, almost jarring. It's the voice of Someone who knows the old scruples and wants to unseat them—not through argument, but through a call Peter's conscience cannot refuse.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter's refusal is quick, almost instinctive. He's a pious man—nothing unholy has entered his mouth. That old faithfulness to the Law is woven into his very bones. The tension here is real; his objection is not timidity but integrity as he understands it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "What God has cleansed, don't you call unclean." The voice speaks again, and it redefines cleanness itself. It's not a soft suggestion; it's a redrawing of the boundary. What was forbidden is now declared clean by God's own word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three times the sheet descends and ascends—the number itself is God's signature, a kind of seal on the lesson. Repetition in Scripture often marks something final, already decided. Peter is not being asked to convince himself; he's being shown a settled truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Caesarea was the Roman provincial capital; these three men came on urgent business—sent by a centurion seeking the word. The timing is no accident. While Peter stands bewildered by the vision, heaven's messenger is already at the gate.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Spirit's instruction is plain: "Go with them, without discriminating." Six brothers came along—witnesses to what Peter was about to do, holding him steady as his old certainties shifted beneath his feet. He didn't walk into that Gentile house alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cornelius tells his own story now: the angel in his house, the command to fetch Peter by name. There's a humility in it—a pagan god-fearer being guided by angelic word to seek out one particular follower of Jesus, asking him to come and speak.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Words by which you will be saved"—the promise is for the whole household. It's both personal and corporate, spoken before Peter has even opened his mouth. The angel speaks as if it's already certain: when Peter speaks, salvation will follow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As Peter began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell—not waited for baptism, not held back, but fell immediately. The same gift as at Pentecost, visible and undeniable. It was the Spirit's verdict before any human council could convene.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter recalls Jesus's words to his disciples about baptism in the Holy Spirit—a promise made before the cross, fulfilled at Pentecost, and now repeated for Gentiles. The Spirit is showing that what began at Pentecost has not aged or narrowed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Who was I, that I could withstand God?" Peter's question is not rhetorical defiance but recognition of his own smallness. He had doubts, scruples, old-covenant instincts—but God moved anyway. To resist would be to stand against the Almighty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Silence, then glory—they held their peace and glorified God. No one hammered Peter further or demanded more proof. The Spirit had already declared the matter settled. And they speak the wonder aloud: God has given Gentiles repentance unto life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The persecution that took Stephen's life scattered the church across Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch—ancient trade routes and cosmopolitan centers. Hardship meant diaspora; diaspora meant the gospel traveling. They carried their faith wherever the wind blew them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Men from Cyprus and Cyrene—not apostles, just scattered believers—arrived in Antioch and spoke to Hellenists about Jesus. They didn't wait for permission or certification. Ordinary disciples, speaking the ordinary news: the Lord is risen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The hand of the Lord was with them"—that phrase names what we can't measure but can see. Great numbers believed and turned. The Lord's hand was working through humble, nameless believers, and Antioch became a beachhead of the faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: News reaches Jerusalem's assembly—the church now had to take notice of what was happening far away. They didn't ignore it, accuse it, or suppress it. Instead, they sent Barnabas, a trusted man known for encouragement, to see and strengthen the work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Barnabas saw the grace of God at work in Antioch and was glad. His joy was not territorial or suspicious but glad. He exhorted them with purpose of heart, calling them to hold fast to the Lord. That's the mark of a true shepherd—he encourages rather than dampens.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Barnabas: a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith. Notice what's absent—ambition, suspicion, need for credit. His character itself became a channel for the Lord's work. Many were added to the Lord. Sometimes the faithful shepherd matters more than the brilliant preacher.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Barnabas went to Tarsus to find Saul—the man still in eclipse, still recovering from his dramatic conversion, still perhaps unsure where he fit. Barnabas didn't forget him. He sought him out. Sometimes the best help is someone who believes in you when you're still finding your feet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul and Barnabas taught together in Antioch for a whole year, and the disciples were first called Christians there. The name itself—followers of Christ—came not from the apostles but from outsiders watching the movement grow. Labels matter; this one stuck because it was true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. The young church hadn't centralized everything in one place; the Spirit's gifts traveled. Prophets appeared as they were needed, carrying both counsel and sometimes hard words.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Agabus stood and prophesied a famine over the whole world, and it happened in Claudius's reign (about 49–50 AD). The prophet spoke God's foreknowledge. His words weren't meant to frighten but to prepare the church to act in love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The disciples determined, "as any had plenty," to send relief to Judean believers. No command was issued. No collection plate was passed. Instead, abundance met need in a quiet mutual obligation—the body caring for itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They sent their gift through Barnabas and Saul to the elders. Readers today hear an echo of the church taking care of its own across distance and difference—a small act that would have felt like a lifeline to those facing hunger. The shape of love is practical and patient.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
